notes.meaning: The story begins by introducing Elkanah from the hill country of Ephraim. He was a Levite, a member of the priestly tribe, living in the town of Ramah. His long family tree shows he came from a respected household. God often starts great works in quiet, faithful families during difficult times.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that early Greek translations read 'a Zuphite' instead of 'Zophim,' suggesting a minor difference in the ancient Hebrew manuscript copying.

notes.meaning: Elkanah had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none, which brought Hannah deep sorrow in that culture. Although having multiple wives was practiced in those days, Scripture repeatedly shows that it caused bitter jealousy and family conflict.

Every year Elkanah traveled with his family to worship and offer sacrifices at Shiloh, where God's tabernacle was set up. Eli was high priest there, and his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, served as priests even though they were corrupt. Despite the wickedness of the priests, Elkanah remained faithful to God and did not use their sins as an excuse to avoid worship.

When Elkanah offered his peace offerings at the feast, he received meat back from the sacrifice to share with his family. He gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to each of her sons and daughters. This shared meal was a time for families to celebrate God's goodness together.

Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion of the meat to show his deep love for her. Even though the Lord had kept her from bearing children, her husband did not value her any less. True love supports a spouse even more during times of hardship.

Peninnah treated Hannah as a rival, constantly mocking and teasing her because she was childless. She tried to make Hannah feel worthless and upset with her lot in life. Selfish jealousy often tempts people to turn someone else's pain into a weapon.

This cruel teasing happened year after year whenever the family went to the house of the Lord. The festive trips became agonizing for Hannah, leaving her in tears and unable to eat. Unresolved family strife can make even holy seasons feel heavy and painful.

Elkanah saw Hannah weeping and gently asked why she was grieving and refusing to eat. He tried to comfort her by asking if his deep love was not better to her than having ten sons. While his words were well-meaning, he could not erase the deep longing of her heart.

After the family finished eating and drinking at Shiloh, Hannah stood up to pray near the sanctuary. The high priest Eli was sitting on a seat by the doorway of the Lord's house, watching the worshippers. Hannah decided to carry her heavy burden directly to God.

Hannah was in bitter distress, weeping deeply as she prayed to the Lord. She did not pretend to be strong or hide her sorrow from God. Bringing our deepest heartache directly to God in honest prayer is always the right choice.

Hannah made a solemn vow, asking the Lord of Hosts to remember her and give her a son. She promised that if God answered, she would give the boy back to Him for his whole life as a Nazirite, someone set apart whose hair would never be cut. She was not just asking for a child to keep, but offering to give him to God's work.

Hannah continued praying earnestly before the Lord for a long time. As she poured out her heart, Eli the priest watched the movement of her mouth. Deep, sincere prayer often takes time and persistence before the Lord.

Hannah was praying silently in her heart, so only her lips moved and no voice was heard. Eli watched her unusual expression and assumed she was drunk from the feast. God hears the silent cries of the heart just as clearly as loud spoken words.

Eli scolded Hannah and told her to stop being drunk and put away her wine. Because misconduct was common around the tabernacle, the old priest assumed the worst about her. Leaders can easily misjudge others when they look only at outward appearances.

Hannah answered Eli with great respect, explaining that she had not had any wine or beer. She told him that she was deeply troubled in spirit and was only pouring out her soul before the Lord. Responding with gentleness when falsely accused helps clear up misunderstandings without anger.

Hannah asked Eli not to think of her as a worthless or wicked woman. She explained that she had been praying out of intense grief and anguish. Honest communication helps others understand the pain behind our actions.

Eli realized he was mistaken and sent Hannah away with a blessing, asking God to grant her request. As high priest, his blessing brought her comfort and assurance. A kind and encouraging word from spiritual leaders can bring peace to an aching soul.

Hannah thanked Eli and asked for his continued favor. She then went back, began eating again, and her face was no longer sad. Because she trusted God with her petition, her peace returned before she ever saw the physical answer.

The family got up early the next morning to worship the Lord before traveling back home to Ramah. After they returned, Elkanah was intimate with Hannah, and the Lord remembered her prayer. God never forgets His people, and He answers at the right time.

In due time Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, which sounds like the Hebrew phrase for 'asked of God,' because she had pleaded for him from the Lord. His name was a lasting testimony to God's faithfulness in answering prayer.

When the time came for the annual festival, Elkanah went up with his household to offer sacrifices and fulfill his own vow. This vow shows that Elkanah agreed with Hannah's promise and offered thanks to God as well. A godly home stands united in honoring commitments made to the Lord.

Hannah chose to stay home until the boy was weaned, saying she would then bring him to live permanently at the tabernacle. Mothers in that culture usually nursed children for two to three years. She wanted Samuel to be ready before leaving him in the Lord's house.

Elkanah supported Hannah's plan, telling her to stay until the child was weaned and praying that the Lord would confirm His word. By law, a husband could cancel his wife's vow, but Elkanah gladly affirmed hers. Husbands and wives honor God when they encourage each other to keep their holy promises.

Once Samuel was weaned, Hannah took him to Shiloh along with a generous offering of an animal, flour, and wine. Even though Samuel was still a young boy, she brought him directly to the house of the Lord. Dedicating what is dearest to us requires real obedience and sacrifice.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Greek and Syriac versions read 'a three-year-old bull' rather than 'three bulls,' matching the single bull mentioned as slaughtered in the next verse.

notes.meaning: They slaughtered the bull as a burnt offering and presented the young child to Eli. Bringing Samuel with a sacrifice showed that his entire future belonged to the Lord. True dedication gives God first place over our closest family bonds.

Hannah greeted Eli respectfully and reminded him that she was the very woman who had stood beside him years earlier weeping in prayer. She wanted him to see the living proof of God's work. Sharing testimonies of answered prayer strengthens the faith of others.

Hannah pointed to the child and told Eli that this was the boy she had prayed for so desperately. She declared that the Lord had granted her the exact petition she had asked of Him. Recognizing that every good gift comes from God keeps our hearts thankful.

Hannah fulfilled her vow by giving Samuel over to the Lord for his whole life, and they worshipped God together there. The boy she had asked from God was now given back to God's service. What we receive from the Lord in grace is always best used when given back to Him.
